newsitem.title: USA: Dingell in no rush to delay new clean air rules.
newsitem.headline: Dingell in no rush to delay new clean air rules.

text.p: Rep. John Dingell said Tuesday there was no need to hurry efforts to block new clean air rules issued two weeks ago by the Environmental Protection Agency because the rules will not be enforced for many years.
The powerful Michigan Democrat is leading efforts to pass a bill to delay the strict new limits on smog and soot for four years because of the potential costs to industry.

"Timing is not really as important as might meet the eye, because first of all the technology's not there," Dingell said at a National Press Club luncheon, referring to the high quality monitors needed to detect soot levels.

Although the new standards were put on the books earlier this month, they will not come into effect until 2004 for smog-forming ozone and until 2005 for fine particles, and will not be enforced until about four years later.
"The administrator of EPA has been rushing around the country saying ... do not worry we are not going to start enforcing them (the rules) soon," he said.
"We have plenty of time," Dingell said. "We will proceed at the best proper speed to win the fight."
House Commerce Committee chairman Thomas Bliley, a Virginia Republican, predicted earlier this month that Dingell would have to secure at least 100 Democratic votes to be able to block the new rules.

"I expect to have the full support of the Republican leadership and very strong support on the Republican side of the aisle," Dingell said, adding that he expected "very strong" support from Democrats and trade unions.

Dingell, who has backed the Clinton administration on many other issues, has been a loud critic of EPA Administrator Carol Browner on the clean air rules, saying she was making false promises about the impacts the rules would have on various sectors, including farms and small businesses.

"These are promises, threats and offers that the agency cannot keep," he said, because states, not the EPA, were in charge of deciding how to meet the clean air standards. "EPA cannot write checks on Greenpeace's account."

The aim of the legislation was to ensure that EPA's effort to bend the Clean Air Act to ease the impact of the new rules, by giving some areas more time to meet the standards, would not leave the federal government and states open to lawsuits, he said.
